newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's exiled king to visit before elections.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's exiled king to visit before elections.

text.p: Bulgaria's exiled King Simeon will visit his homeland on Tuesday to mark the anniversary of the country's first constitution, four days before parliamentary elections, the state news agency BTA said on Sunday.

King Simeon, who left Bulgaria as a child in 1946 and lives in Madrid, will arrive in the town of Veliko Tarnovo on Tuesday afternoon and will leave the following morning, BTA quoted his spokeswoman as saying.
The 1879 Tarnovo constitution, which marks its 118th anniversary this week, was the first to be drawn up in the newly-independent state after 500 years of Ottoman rule.

King Simeon has been careful to stay out of politics, though at the height of demonstrations against the former Socialist government in January he added his voice to calls for early parliamentary elections as a way out of the crisis.
BTA said the king would use a special plane to fly into the small airport at Gorna Oriahovitsa, bypassing the capital.

Now 59, Simeon fled Bulgaria in 1946 after the Soviet Army installed a puppet communist regime. He returned to Bulgaria for the first time for a three-week visit in May last year and was mobbed by an ecstatic flag-waving public.
Simeon has never renounced his claim to the throne. As a Saxe-Coburg, he is related to other European royal families, including Britain's House of Windsor.
The balding, bearded monarch is respected even by republicans as a serious, hard-working businessman who eschews the playboy lifestyle of some exiled royals.
Many Bulgarians see restoration of the monarchy as a possible way out of the country's political and economic crisis, and several monarchist political parties are contesting Saturday's elections.

Simeon has said that he is the king of all Bulgarians and does not favour any one group, but he received leaders of the Alliance for National Salvation, a coalition grouping the main monarchist parties and the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms, in Madrid last week. Pictures of the king with coalition leaders appear on their election posters.
The Union of Democratic Forces, which is expected to win a majority in Saturday's elections, is seen as more sympathetic to the monarchists' cause than the previous Socialist administration.

When the king visited last year, he did not meet the then Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov, but he did meet the present interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski, who was mayor of Sofia at the time.
